flags.finding: The musical composition 'Hallelujah', written and composed by Leonard Cohen, is featured as a plot-critical diegetic cue across scenes S002, S004 (played at the funeral service), and S011 (broadcast across the harbor during the boat burning). Synchronizing a copyrighted musical composition with audiovisual images requires a worldwide synchronization license from the composition's publisher, Sony/ATV Music Publishing (Sony Music Publishing / BMI). Unlicensed synchronization of this iconic composition will prevent commercial release and delivery.

citations.title: Sound Legal: Smart Tips for Clearing Music in Your Film
citations.excerpt: Copyright offers creators control over how their music is used, while synchronization rights let you pair a composition with your visuals. Master use rights apply to the specific recording of a song, and you’ll typically need both sync and master use licenses for commercial tracks.

remedy.detail: Negotiate a worldwide, all-media synchronization license with Sony/ATV Music Publishing (licensing fee estimate $25,000–$75,000+ for indie feature rights; ownership splits unverified — confirm via Songview before negotiating). For budget-constrained indie productions, use a temp track during post-production and either (a) replace the cue with an original composition or a track licensed from an indie artist / production music library ($500–$2,500 labor/licensing), or (b) drop the cue and rewrite the scripted dialogue in S002. Avoid commissioning a sound-alike that mimics Leonard Cohen's arrangement to prevent right of publicity or derivative copyright disputes.

# **Built by Filmmakers: Premium On-Set Notepads for Every Production.**
## Why music is different from almost everything else you license
Think of it this way. The composition is the song “Hallelujah” as Leonard Cohen wrote it. The master is Jeff Buckley’s particular recording of it.
If you want to use Jeff Buckley’s recording in your film, you need permission from whoever controls the composition AND permission from whoever controls that specific recording. Two rights, two owners, two licenses.

## The two licenses you need
Because there are two copyrights, there are two licenses.
A **synchronization license** (a “sync” license) grants you the right to synchronize the musical composition with your visual images, to marry the song to your picture. It comes from the composition’s owner, usually the music publisher.
A **master use license** grants you the right to use the specific sound recording. It comes from the master’s owner, usually the record label.
